title: AWS CWI Exam Prep in Denver, CO: 6-Day Course
description: Six-day AWS CWI exam prep for Denver and the Front Range: online or at your shop, for energy, pipeline, refinery and construction welding inspectors.
h1: AWS CWI Exam Prep in Denver: Six Days for Front Range Energy and Construction Inspectors
html:
Denver sits at the meeting point of two welding economies. To the north and east are the oil and gas fields, gathering systems and processing plants of the plains; in and around the city are the cranes, bridges, transit lines and industrial buildings of a metro that has grown steadily for two decades. A welding inspector on the Front Range might spend a spring on a compressor station near Greeley and an autumn on a downtown tower. Atlantis NDT's six-day course prepares welders, fitters, QC staff, NDT technicians and engineers for the AWS Certified Welding Inspector examination in either setting. Someone preparing alone works online from a written plan, using course materials and practice questions, and can put any question to an instructor along the way. Companies with several candidates can have the six days delivered on their own premises. Request a Denver quote to see how it would work for you.

The certification is AWS's to give, not ours. AWS administers the examination, scores it, and decides who receives the CWI. Atlantis helps candidates prepare. It certifies nobody, has no knowledge of what is on a given exam, and is neither approved nor endorsed by AWS. The course's practice questions are written by Atlantis to the subject areas AWS publishes, and none of them is taken from an AWS exam.

Denver as the Mountain West's practical exam city

One fact shapes CWI planning across the whole region. AWS gives Part B, the practical, only at its own seminar locations, and on its current US list Denver is the one city in the Rocky Mountain states. There is no listed location in Utah, Wyoming, Montana, New Mexico, Arizona or Nevada. Candidates from Salt Lake City, Cheyenne, Albuquerque and the oil towns of Wyoming and the Dakotas often come to Denver for the practical, while Front Range candidates can usually sit it without an overnight stay.

The other two parts are more flexible. AWS delivers Part A and Part C as computer-based tests at Prometric centres, which a candidate books after AWS accepts the application and issues an eligibility code. A Denver candidate might take Parts A and C at a nearby Prometric centre on one date and Part B at the AWS seminar location on another. Locations and dates move during the year, so confirm the current arrangements on aws.org before asking for time off.

Oil, gas and pipelines north and east of the city

The Denver-Julesburg Basin stretches across the plains north and east of the metro, and its development has filled Weld, Adams and neighbouring counties with well pads, gathering lines, compressor stations, gas processing plants and storage. That infrastructure is welded steel. Gathering and transmission pipeline welds are generally made and inspected to API 1104, and new facilities bring in piping, vessel and tank work along with the lines themselves. Midstream companies, pipeline construction contractors and inspection firms on the Front Range hire welding inspectors to check welder qualification, joint preparation, alignment, preheat where required, and the finished cap and root before radiography or ultrasonic testing is done by the appropriate contractor.

Federal rules administered by PHMSA cover interstate and many intrastate gas and hazardous liquid lines, and the state carries out pipeline safety oversight for intrastate gas systems. Those rules incorporate API 1104 by reference, but the edition they incorporate is the 21st, while AWS uses the 22nd edition for Part C. A pipeline candidate should learn the 22nd edition well for the exam and keep track of what changed between editions, because a Colorado project may specify either. Read the API 1104 standard summary for the document itself, and the explainer on welding procedure and welder qualification records for how pipeline qualification departs from structural practice. For the volumetric methods that follow visual acceptance on pipelines, see UT for pipelines.

Refining and process plants in Commerce City

Just north of downtown, a refinery complex in Commerce City runs ongoing maintenance and periodic turnarounds, and gas processing plants on the plains have their own repair programs. Plant piping there generally follows ASME B31.3. The welding procedures are the plant's or the piping contractor's, qualified under ASME Section IX, and Atlantis has no hand in writing or qualifying them. A welding inspector there confirms that each welder holds the right qualification for the procedure in use, that fit-up and preheat are right, and that finished welds pass visual examination before they move on to NDT and pressure testing.

B31.3 is one of the Part C books AWS offers, and it suits candidates who expect to stay in plant work. Its layout takes practice, and the course's code day spends its time on where the examination and acceptance rules live and how to move between the text and its tables without losing minutes. Atlantis also runs refinery-focused NDT training for Denver for plant staff who need methods beyond visual inspection.

Building, bridges and transit along the Front Range

The metro's construction market keeps structural steel fabricators, erectors and testing agencies busy: office and residential towers in and around downtown, hospital and university buildings, warehouses along the I-70 and I-25 corridors, and industrial buildings for manufacturers. Structural steel welding on these projects is done to AWS D1.1, and building departments require special inspection under their adopted building codes, so independent agencies place welding inspectors on most significant steel jobs. Each jurisdiction decides which credentials it accepts for that role, and the AWS CWI is widely used for it.

Transportation work adds bridge steel. Highway structures built for the state and local agencies are generally fabricated to AWS D1.5, which is stricter than D1.1 on procedure qualification, consumable control and fracture-critical members. Transit construction adds its own structures and stations. A Denver candidate who expects to move between building and bridge work usually takes Part C in D1.1, which AWS offers in its 2020 edition, then studies D1.5 once certified; a candidate working full time in a bridge shop may prefer D1.5 for the exam itself.

Front Range weather tests discipline as much as knowledge. Winter cold fronts can drop temperatures sharply within hours, spring brings wind that strips shielding gas from a gas-shielded weld, and summer afternoons bring storms. D1.1 sets limits on welding in low temperatures and wet or windy conditions, and an inspector on an open deck has to stop work, require protection, or check that windscreens and heating are in place, then record the conditions.

Aerospace and advanced manufacturing

Colorado has a large aerospace and space industry concentrated in the Denver suburbs and along the Front Range, supported by machine shops, weld shops and test facilities. Welding on flight and space hardware generally follows AWS D17.1 or a customer specification, and inspection there is about weld class, tight acceptance limits and parts traceability. D17.1 (2024 edition) is on the AWS Part C list, and inspectors who plan to stay with flight hardware often take the exam in it. For the NDT side of aerospace work, see UT in aviation.

What the AWS examination involves

Each of the three parts is scored separately, and AWS requires at least 72 percent on every one. Part A, Fundamentals, poses 150 questions on welding processes, metallurgy, testing methods, symbols, procedure documents, safety and calculations. Part B, Practical, uses hands-on activities and 46 questions to test whether a candidate can measure and evaluate welds with real tools and work from procedure and qualification records. Part C, Code Application, is open-book: 50 to 65 questions in the code chosen when applying. Speed in that one book matters more than wide reading, which is why the course commits a full day to it.

Six days arranged for Front Range candidates

For the detailed daily breakdown, open the national six-day CWI course outline. The opening pair of days rebuilds fundamentals: processes, joint design, welding symbols according to AWS A2.4 and terminology according to AWS A3.0 on day one; metallurgy, mechanical testing, how discontinuities form, destructive and nondestructive testing, safety and professional ethics on day two. Day three works on the measuring, gauging and visual acceptance skills Part B checks. Day four is a guided tour of the chosen code book. Day five puts candidates through timed mock papers for all three parts, then reviews each error. Day six targets the weakest areas, sets an exam-day plan and checks the application file.

Field schedules on the plains rarely leave room for fixed class times, so individuals follow the plan online at their own pace. Enrolment opens access right away, nothing is scheduled, and the instructor picks up questions whenever a topic will not settle. For a fabricator, pipeline contractor or plant with several candidates, Atlantis can deliver all six days at the employer's facility. On day three the group practises with the company's own fillet and undercut gauges, high-low gauges, calipers and production welds, which is closer to Part B than any set of photographs. Atlantis does not provide replica kits and has no training centre in Colorado; on-site delivery always means the employer's premises. Atlantis also offers corporate NDT training in Denver on the same on-site model.

Two free tools help between sessions. Candidates can firm up Part A's testing content with the free NDT practice tests, and rehearse a full inspection sequence in the welding workshop scenario of Practical NDT. The part-by-part analysis of CWI results shows where candidates tend to lose points.

Are you eligible? A quick check against AWS QC1

AWS eligibility comes from QC1, the specification for certifying welding inspectors, which AWS currently lists in its 2016 edition with Amendment 1. Find the line that matches your highest education and compare it with your years of welding-based work. A welding engineering or welding engineering technology bachelor's degree needs one year. An associate degree (welding, engineering, engineering technology or a physical science) needs two. Coursework toward a welding bachelor's degree needs three. Completed trade or vocational training needs four. A high school diploma or approved equivalent needs five. Schooling to eighth grade needs nine, and anything less needs twelve.

The application must be backed by an employment verification form, a completed AWS Visual Acuity Exam Form showing that you passed the vision examination, and photo identification meeting AWS's rules. Pipeline welders and fitters should list the operators, contractors, codes and roles for each job; AWS decides what counts as welding-based experience, and specific descriptions help. The course reviews the file on its final day, but the application, the vision examination and the fees paid to AWS remain the candidate's responsibility. The article on CWI certification requirements goes further.

Denver welding schools and the AWS Colorado Section

AWS members in the metro belong to the Colorado Section, part of AWS District 20; the Southern Colorado Section covers the Colorado Springs and Pueblo end of the Front Range. Section meetings bring together inspectors, educators, fabricators and suppliers, and they are a sensible place to meet someone who passed recently, learn which employers support candidates, and find out how local technical programs count toward recertification hours.

Several schools feed the trade. Red Rocks Community College teaches welding at its Lakewood campus, with certificates in shielded metal arc, gas metal arc, flux-cored, gas tungsten arc and oxy-fuel welding and cutting, plus an associate of applied science in welding; the college says students can earn entry-level AWS welder certification on completion. Emily Griffith Technical College in downtown Denver runs a Welding 1 program that covers stick, MIG, flux-cored and TIG welding, cutting, blueprint reading and weld inspection and testing, aimed at the skills for the student AWS D1.1 certification, with credits that transfer toward an associate degree at Front Range Community College. A graduate who adds several years of structural, pipe or production welding has an experience record that suits a CWI application, and an associate degree shortens the experience AWS requires.

Keeping the CWI and building on it

The CWI runs nine years. AWS requires renewal at the third and sixth years, each time confirming you have had no gap longer than two years in practice or employment during the previous three. At the end of the cycle you recertify through a route AWS accepts; taking Part B again and completing 80 professional development hours are both on the list. Senior CWI is the next step for experienced inspectors, covered in the SCWI pathway article.

Pipeline, refinery and structural specifications on the Front Range often require magnetic particle or ultrasonic examination after the welding inspector accepts a weld visually, so many Denver CWIs add NDT methods. Atlantis teaches NDT to ASNT SNT-TC-1A, a scheme in which the employer certifies staff through its written practice, never the training provider. Useful next steps include VT Level 2 training, UT training and the NDT training options for Denver. API 510, 570 and 653 preparation is outside Atlantis's scope. The welding inspector vs NDT technician comparison sets out the difference between the roles. Companies that need field inspection can see weld inspection services in Denver and visual testing in Denver.

Asking for a Denver quote

Let us know whether the request is for you alone or for a group, what each candidate does now, approximate years of welding-based experience, the Part C book in mind (API 1104, B31.3, D1.1, D1.5 and D17.1 cover most Front Range work) and the target exam window. For on-site delivery, include the facility address, site safety or orientation requirements, and whether gauges, production welds and a quiet room are available. For the AWS side of the budget, check the charges posted on aws.org, then add travel and books in the CWI budgeting guide. Send the Denver request; we reply within one business day.

Candidates from the wider region may also find the Salt Lake City page, the Phoenix page and the Kansas City page useful.

faq.q: Is Denver an AWS location for the CWI practical exam?
faq.a: Yes. AWS currently names Denver among its US seminar cities, where Part B is held, and no other listed city lies in the Rocky Mountain states. Parts A and C are taken at Prometric centres. Check aws.org for dates.

faq.q: Which Part C book suits Front Range pipeline work?
faq.a: API 1104, which AWS offers in its 22nd edition. The federal pipeline rules still incorporate the 21st edition, so check which edition each project specifies after you pass.

faq.q: Which Part C book suits refinery and gas plant inspectors?
faq.a: ASME B31.3 is the usual choice for plant piping. Structural inspectors generally pick AWS D1.1, bridge shop staff D1.5 and aerospace inspectors D17.1.

faq.q: Does Atlantis have a classroom in Denver?
faq.a: No. Individuals study online and get answers from an instructor; employers can host the six days at their own facility. Atlantis has no classroom or office in Colorado.

faq.q: How long does the course take?
faq.a: It is a six-day course. On-site groups normally run the days consecutively, and online candidates fit the same content around field rotations.

faq.q: Who certifies me as a CWI?
faq.a: AWS. It runs the examination and grants the CWI once you satisfy QC1 eligibility, pass its vision examination and pass Parts A, B and C. Atlantis provides preparation, not certification.

faq.q: I came up through Red Rocks or Emily Griffith. How much experience do I need?
faq.a: It depends on the credential. An associate degree in welding reduces the AWS requirement to two years of welding-based experience; a certificate or completed vocational courses generally falls under the four-year line; a high school diploma alone needs five years.

faq.q: Can a pipeline contractor host the course at its yard?
faq.a: Yes. Use the quote form to give the headcount, each person's job, the code book they will use, the yard address and any orientation the site requires. We reply within one business day.

faq.q: Are the practice questions copies of AWS exam questions?
faq.a: No. Atlantis writes them to the subject areas AWS publishes. AWS exam content is confidential.

faq.q: What NDT training pairs well with a CWI in Colorado?
faq.a: Start with visual testing, then add ultrasonic or magnetic particle methods for pipeline and plant work; Atlantis teaches them to ASNT SNT-TC-1A, and your employer certifies you. See NDT training for Denver.
